title: WHY DID GOD FORBID A MAN FROM “UNCOVERING A WOMAN’S NAKEDNESS”? THE DISTURBING TRUTH HIDDEN IN LEVITICUS 18:6
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD FORBID A MAN FROM “UNCOVERING A WOMAN’S NAKEDNESS”? THE DISTURBING TRUTH HIDDEN IN LEVITICUS 18:6
One ancient Hebrew expression. One command that modern readers often misunderstand. And one uncomfortable truth about sex, family, secrecy, and the holiness of God that still confronts us today.
There are Bible verses that comfort you.
There are Bible verses that strengthen you.
And then there are Bible verses that make you stop reading, stare at the page, and whisper, “Lord… what exactly are You saying?”
Leviticus 18:6 is one of them.
Because when God told Israel not to approach someone to “uncover nakedness,” He was not simply giving instructions about clothing.
He was addressing something far more intimate.
Something that could destroy families.
Something that could turn trust into betrayal, affection into exploitation, and what should have been a place of safety into a lifetime of wounds.
And here is what makes this passage so important.
If you misunderstand the expression, you may misunderstand the command. But if you understand the Hebrew, you begin to see why God spoke so seriously about sexual boundaries.
The verse says:
“None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD.”
— Leviticus 18:6, KJV
Read those final words again.
“I am the LORD.”
Not merely, “This is socially unacceptable.”
Not merely, “This is how your ancestors behaved.”
God placed His own authority behind the command.
But why?
What does “uncover nakedness” actually mean?
And why does a passage written thousands of years ago still matter to people struggling with sexual temptation, hidden shame, family wounds, and the longing to be made clean?
The answer begins in the Hebrew.
And it may challenge some things you have heard preached about this verse.
In the original Hebrew, the central expression is:
לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה
Legal·lōth ʿerwāh — “to uncover nakedness.”
The verb comes from the Hebrew root גלה (g-l-h), meaning “to uncover,” “to reveal,” or “to expose.”
The noun עֶרְוָה (ʿerwāh) refers to nakedness, particularly intimate or sexual nakedness, and can carry the sense of shameful exposure depending on the context.
But here is the critical distinction.
In Leviticus 18, this is not merely a description of someone accidentally seeing another person without clothes.
It is a sexual expression used within a series of prohibitions against unlawful sexual relations.
And we know this because the surrounding verses explain what the expression means in context.
Leviticus 18:7 forbids uncovering the nakedness of one's father or mother, then specifically identifies the mother's nakedness.
Leviticus 18:8 prohibits uncovering the nakedness of one's father's wife, explaining that her nakedness is connected to the father's.
Leviticus 18:14 speaks of an uncle's nakedness and immediately clarifies the prohibition by referring to approaching his wife.
Leviticus 18:20 then speaks explicitly of sexual intercourse with a neighbor's wife.
The chapter is not a random collection of rules about looking at bodies.
It is addressing sexual relationships that God forbade.
The wording in Leviticus 18:6 is even more revealing when we examine its opening phrase:
אִישׁ אִישׁ אֶל־כָּל־שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ לֹא תִקְרְבוּ לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה
A close rendering is:
“None of you shall approach anyone who is a close relative to uncover nakedness.”
The expression שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ (she'er besaro) refers to someone of one's own flesh, a close relative.
And לֹא תִקְרְבוּ (lo tiqrevu) means “you shall not approach” in this construction.
The command concerns approaching a close relative for a prohibited sexual purpose.

This matters because the verse is sometimes quoted as though God were forbidding all physical closeness between men and women, or as though every instance of seeing someone's nakedness automatically constituted the specific offense described here.
That goes beyond what this passage actually says.
The biblical context identifies the issue as forbidden sexual intimacy, especially within relationships of close kinship.

And the original wording of verse 6 does not simply say “a woman.” Its prohibition is expressed broadly in relation to close relatives, with the following verses specifying the forbidden relationships.
That is why careful interpretation matters.
We do not honor Scripture by making it say more than it says.
We honor Scripture by listening carefully to what God actually revealed.
And when we do, something powerful emerges.
God was placing boundaries around relationships in which trust, family responsibility, and sexual conduct could become dangerously entangled.
Imagine a home where the people who should protect you are the very people you fear.
Imagine growing up around someone whose affection comes with an expectation you never agreed to.
Imagine carrying a secret for years because speaking the truth might divide the family.
Imagine being told to remain silent to preserve a reputation while your own heart quietly falls apart.
For some people, those words are not hypothetical.
They describe childhood.
They describe family gatherings.
They describe memories they have spent years trying to bury.
And this is where we must handle the passage with both conviction and compassion.
God's prohibition of sexual wrongdoing must never be twisted into condemnation of the person who was violated.
A child who has been abused has not become guilty of the abuser's sin.
A person who was coerced has not forfeited their worth before God.
Someone who was assaulted does not become spiritually dirty because another person committed evil against them.

Scripture itself recognizes the moral distinction between wrongdoing and victimization. Deuteronomy 22:25–27, in its discussion of sexual violence, explicitly places guilt upon the attacker rather than the victim in the case it describes.
That distinction matters.
Because some people have been carrying shame that belongs to someone else's actions.
Some have been told to forgive without being allowed to speak.
Some have been pressured to protect an abuser in the name of family unity.
Some have even been made to believe that exposing wrongdoing dishonors God.
But hiding abuse is not holiness.
Protecting a reputation at the expense of the vulnerable is not righteousness.
And forgiveness does not require silence, continued access to an abuser, or the abandonment of justice.
The God who commands holiness is also the God who loves justice.
Psalm 82:3–4 calls for justice for the weak and the fatherless and for the deliverance of the afflicted and needy.
And the Lord Jesus spoke with extraordinary seriousness about causing vulnerable little ones to stumble (Matthew 18:6).
So when we read Leviticus 18, we must not reduce its commands to a cold list of forbidden acts.
We must recognize the moral seriousness of the relationships involved.
The family was never meant to become a hiding place for sexual exploitation.
The home was never meant to become a sanctuary for predators.
And the authority entrusted to a parent, guardian, or relative was never permission to take what God had forbidden.
But there is another side to this passage that we cannot ignore.
Because not every sexual sin begins with violence.
Some begin with a secret conversation.
An inappropriate attachment.
A boundary deliberately crossed.
A desire entertained until the conscience grows quieter.
Someone says, “We didn't mean for it to happen.”
Someone else says, “Nobody will ever know.”
And sometimes those words become the doorway to betrayal.
The Bible does not teach that every desire is itself the same as a completed act. But Jesus warns that deliberately cultivating lust is a serious matter of the heart (Matthew 5:27–28).
Sin can begin long before it becomes publicly visible.
That is why God's boundaries are not merely concerned with what other people can discover.
They are concerned with what we are becoming when nobody is watching.
And perhaps that is the uncomfortable question this passage leaves with us.
Not simply, “What did ancient Israel do?”
But, “What am I allowing in my life that I already know I should surrender?”
Maybe it is a relationship you keep defending even though you know its intimacy has crossed a moral boundary.
Maybe it is pornography that has slowly reshaped the way you see other people.
Maybe it is an emotional affair you have renamed “friendship” because admitting the truth would demand change.
Maybe it is a secret that has survived only because you have become skilled at hiding it.
Or perhaps you are reading this from the opposite side of the wound.
You did not choose what happened.
You did not invite the betrayal.
And you have spent years wondering whether God sees you differently because of it.
Please hear this.
Your suffering is not proof that God has rejected you.
The Lord sees what people conceal.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
— KJV
That promise does not mean every wound disappears immediately.
It does not mean trauma is healed by pretending nothing happened.
And it does not mean a person must avoid professional care, trusted support, or lawful protection.
But it does mean that suffering does not place you beyond the reach of God's compassion.
Now consider something else.
Why did God give Israel these commands in the first place?
Leviticus 18:3 provides part of the answer.
Israel was warned not to imitate the practices of Egypt, where they had lived, or Canaan, where they were going.
God was forming a people whose lives would reflect His character rather than simply mirror the surrounding cultures.
Then comes the repeated declaration:
“I am the LORD.”
That statement appears throughout the chapter.
It is the foundation of the command.
Israel's sexual conduct was not supposed to be governed merely by appetite, opportunity, custom, or convenience.
It was to be governed by the God who had delivered them.
And notice the order.
God had already brought Israel out of Egypt before giving these instructions at Sinai.
Obedience was not the price they paid to make God their Redeemer.
It was part of how a redeemed people were called to live.
That distinction prepares us to understand the Gospel.
Because the Bible's story does not end with humanity being commanded to be holy.
It moves toward the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
And that brings us to Jesus Christ.
Think about the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She was accused of adultery.
She stood surrounded by people ready to condemn her.
Her wrongdoing had become public spectacle.
And Jesus refused to participate in their trap.
He confronted the accusers and then spoke directly to the woman.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
— John 8:11, KJV
Those words must be understood together.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
“Go, and sin no more.”
Mercy did not become permission to continue in sin.
And the call to change did not erase the mercy being offered.
Jesus did not announce that adultery was suddenly righteous.
He also refused to treat the woman as though her failure were the entirety of her identity.
This is one of the breathtaking realities of the Gospel.
Jesus does not need to pretend sin is harmless in order to show mercy to sinners.
He is full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
He calls people out of darkness because He loves them, not because He delights in humiliating them.
And the cross reveals just how seriously God takes both sin and redemption.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
— KJV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had perfected ourselves.
Not after every secret had been resolved.
Not after we had become worthy of salvation through our own efforts.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
But that grace is never presented as a license to keep doing evil.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
Paul's answer is emphatic.
“God forbid.”
Grace does not merely offer relief from guilt.
It calls us into a new life.
And this is where the theme of Gospel Warrior becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Not because the past never happened.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because forgiveness makes accountability unnecessary.
But because the finished work of Jesus Christ makes repentance, forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a transformed life possible.
The Gospel does not erase historical facts.
It changes what sin and shame are allowed to say about a person who belongs to Christ.
Consider the Apostle Paul.
Before his conversion, he persecuted the church.
He later acknowledged the seriousness of his former life.
Yet the grace of God transformed him into a servant of the very Christ he had opposed (1 Timothy 1:12–16).
His past remained part of his testimony.
But it was no longer the final word.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needs to understand.
If you have sinned sexually, do not excuse it.
Do not call evil love.
Do not blame another person for choices that were yours.
Do not use God's forgiveness as a reason to avoid confession, restitution, or accountability.
If you have harmed someone, genuine repentance includes stopping the harm, respecting their safety and boundaries, and accepting appropriate consequences.
But do not imagine that your sin is more powerful than the blood of Jesus Christ.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— KJV
The promise is not that confession makes wrongdoing insignificant.
The promise is that God is faithful to forgive and cleanse those who come to Him.
And if you are the person who was harmed, you are not required to describe yourself as the guilty one in order to receive God's care.
You may need healing rather than repentance for the harm done against you.
You may need protection rather than another demand to remain quiet.
You may need people who will listen, believe you, help you find safety, and walk beside you patiently.
Jesus does not ask the wounded to call evil good.
He is the light of the world (John 8:12).
And light reveals what darkness tries to hide.
There is another Hebrew expression worth understanding.
In Genesis 2:24, the Bible says that a man shall leave his father and mother, hold fast to his wife, and that they shall become בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad) — “one flesh.”
This is not the same expression used in Leviticus 18:6.
But the relationship between the passages is illuminating.
Genesis presents marriage as a covenantal union in which two become one flesh.
Leviticus establishes boundaries against sexual unions that violate God's commands.
And Jesus Himself returns to Genesis 2:24 when teaching about marriage in Matthew 19:4–6.
He does not treat the body as meaningless.
He does not treat sexual intimacy as a trivial appetite.
He places marriage within the purposes of the Creator.
This does not mean every person must marry to live a faithful Christian life. Jesus and Paul both affirm the dignity of unmarried life (Matthew 19:10–12; 1 Corinthians 7).
It means that our bodies and relationships matter to God.
And for believers, that truth becomes even more personal.
First Corinthians 6:19–20 teaches that the believer's body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and calls Christians to glorify God in their bodies.
Your body is not spiritually irrelevant.
The way you treat other people is not spiritually irrelevant.
What you do in secret is not spiritually irrelevant.
And neither is the dignity of the person standing before you.
That person is not an object to consume.
Not a secret to exploit.
Not a body without a soul.
Not an opportunity to satisfy desire without responsibility.
They are a human being made in the image of God.
This is why sexual holiness cannot be reduced to avoiding a list of forbidden acts.

It also involves learning to love without exploiting, exercising self-control, honoring commitments, respecting boundaries, and refusing to treat another person's vulnerability as an invitation to sin.
And if that sounds impossible because of the life you have lived, remember what the Apostle Paul wrote to believers in Corinth.
After describing serious sins from which people needed to turn, he said:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”
— 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
“Such were some of you.”
There is hope in those words.
Not because the sins were imaginary.
But because the grace of God had begun a real transformation.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not through human achievement.
But in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of God.
That is what makes Christianity different from a message of mere self-improvement.
The Gospel does not simply say, “Try harder to become a better person.”
It announces what God has done through Jesus Christ to reconcile sinners to Himself and calls those who believe to walk in the new life His grace provides.
And now, after everything we have seen in Leviticus 18:6, perhaps the question has changed.
We began by asking why God forbade someone from approaching a close relative to uncover nakedness.
We discovered that the Hebrew describes prohibited sexual intimacy, not merely the accidental sight of an unclothed body.
We saw how the surrounding chapter establishes boundaries around family relationships and sexual conduct.
We saw that God's commands must never be used to shame victims or conceal abuse.
And we saw that the holiness revealed in the Law points us toward our need for the grace and redemption found in Jesus Christ.
But now the question becomes personal.
What will you do with the truth?
Will you keep defending what Scripture calls sin?
Will you continue hiding something that needs to be brought into the light?
Will you keep allowing shame to tell you that Christ cannot receive a repentant sinner?
Will you keep carrying blame for something another person did to you?
Or will you begin bringing the truth before the Lord?
Not with a rehearsed religious performance.
Not with impressive words.
But with honesty.
“Lord Jesus, I need You.”
Sometimes those five words are where a life begins to change.
Maybe you need to confess.
Maybe you need to seek help.
Maybe you need to end a sinful relationship.
Maybe you need to establish a boundary that should have existed years ago.
Maybe you need to tell a trusted person about the harm you have endured.
Maybe you need to believe that the Savior who died and rose again is able to receive you even after everything you have done.
Whatever the next faithful step looks like, do not confuse hiding with healing.
And do not confuse religious appearance with genuine transformation.
Jesus came to save sinners.
And He is worthy of more than the version of ourselves we allow other people to see.
You do not owe strangers the details of your pain. A few sincere words can still open the door to encouragement, prayer, and Christian fellowship.
And perhaps there is someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message.
Someone who has misunderstood this passage.
Someone struggling with sexual temptation.
Someone who believes their past has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who has been hurt by people who were supposed to protect them.
You may never know whose private prayer is answered when biblical truth reaches them at the right moment.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people move beyond inspirational quotations into meaningful engagement with Scripture, repentance, spiritual growth, and a deeper relationship with Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning accessible to people who are hungry for the Word, including those who may not have the means to purchase Christian books.
And that work needs people who believe it is worth sustaining.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward for financial contributions (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But if you believe this ministry is faithfully serving the Gospel and you have the ability to support it, your voluntary generosity can be one meaningful expression of stewardship.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, God loves a cheerful giver, not someone pressured into giving.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
But through a shared desire to help more people encounter the truth of Scripture.
These products are simply an additional way to express gratitude. They are not the reason anyone should give.
The greater purpose is to help sustain the ministry and encourage continued growth in Christ.
And if you cannot contribute financially, you are still welcome here.
The free biblical resources remain part of our mission, because the Gospel is not merchandise and the love of Christ is not for sale.
Before you leave, remember where this journey began.
One ancient command.
One Hebrew expression.
One warning about forbidden intimacy.
But behind that command was the holiness of a God who cares about what human beings do with their bodies, their relationships, their responsibilities, and the trust placed in their hands.
And beyond the Law, we see the Savior who came not to abolish God's righteousness but to fulfill the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 5:17).
The same Jesus who calls sinners to repentance offers forgiveness through His death and resurrection.
The same Jesus who exposes darkness offers light.
The same Jesus who tells us to turn away from sin also invites the weary and burdened to come to Him (Matthew 11:28).
So do not leave this article merely knowing what an ancient Hebrew phrase means.
Leave knowing that God's Word deserves to be understood in context.
Leave remembering that holiness and compassion belong together.
Leave refusing to excuse abuse, exploit another person's vulnerability, or make peace with hidden sin.
And above all, leave looking to Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest hope of the Gospel is not that we can rewrite our own history.
It is that Jesus Christ can redeem people whose histories they cannot change.
The past may still carry your fingerprints, your tears, or your scars—but it does not have the authority to write the final sentence over a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
